items.title: Rise in energy bills in Britain to £2,166 is ‘an impossible high’ for millions of households; stocks tumble as AI rally fizzles – business live
items.summary:
Regulator Ofgem announces that the typical annual gas and electricity bill will rise by 26% in January – described as ‘deeply worrying’ by campaigners

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Typical annual energy bills in Great Britain will rise by 26% in January to £2,166, the energy regulator has announced – which was immediately described as “an impossible high” and “deeply worrying” by charities.

January’s price cap hike will push energy bills to an impossible high for millions already struggling to afford basic essentials.

The [government’s] £100 Household Energy Payment is welcome but these sky high prices mean it will be swallowed up in less than two weeks for most households. People on low incomes risk falling into deeper debt, while those on prepayment meters could be left without heat and power in the dead of winter because they can’t afford to top up.

Conflict in the Middle East continues to drive energy costs higher, and we know this price increase will be a worry for many households as winter approaches.

We urge anyone who is struggling to afford their energy bills to reach out to their supplier, who must offer appropriate support and advice – we are writing to suppliers today to remind them of their obligations and ensure they are ready to provide that support.

The timing could hardly be worse. These higher prices will hit in January, immediately after Christmas and during the coldest months of the year, when older…
items.t: Rise in energy bills in Britain to £2,166 is ‘an impossible high’ for millions of households; stocks tumble as AI rally fizzles – business live

items.title: Backed by Samsung, SK Hynix, and the Korean government, Rebellions CEO Sunghyun Park wants to prove sovereign AI pays off
items.summary:
Few corporate rivalries are as fierce as the one between Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The world’s leading manufacturer of memory chips and the world’s leading manufacturer of high-bandwidth memory, respectively, are fighting for the title of South Korea’s most valuable company. In one area, though, the two are on the same team: Both back Rebellions, the $2.3 billion chip startup cofounded by Sunghyun Park—a veteran of Intel , SpaceX, and Morgan Stanley—that fronts South Korea’s push for sovereign silicon or AI chips that don’t depend on market leader Nvidia or any other U.S. or Chinese company.

Park’s company sits at the center of government policy. “AI requires huge capital and huge talent,” he says. “Instead of having multiple players compete, the Korean government said, ‘We need one champion. SK Hynix , please help him. Samsung, please help him. SK Telecom, KT’—top two data center companies—‘please become Rebellions’ customers.’”

Rebellions may be the clearest test of whether sovereign AI can produce something more than an expensive also-ran . Korea is funneling its best resources toward Rebellions: Samsung’s foundries, SK Hynix’s memory , and government money. The Korea National Growth Fund co-led Rebellions’ $400 million round in March.

Will it pay off? Rebellions eventually wants public investors to back a risky bet on a chip startup in a market that—for now—is skeptical of AI stocks. Still, Park is hopeful. Rebellions’ backers make it “more powerful compared to any other player in the United States,” he says. But market volatility and a wave of shelved data…
items.t: Backed by Samsung, SK Hynix, and the Korean government, Rebellions CEO Sunghyun Park wants to prove sovereign AI pays off

items.title: ‘We’re begging’: DOGE slashed federal workforce to its lowest in 60 years, and the Trump administration says it still can’t recruit Gen Z workers
items.summary:
The Trump administration is doubling down on efforts to hire young people, but the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) campaign to cull the federal workforce may now be hampering that goal.

On Nov. 12, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor visited Texas Christian University and spoke with students. The reason? Recruiting the next generation of future government workers. 

It’s a big problem: People younger than 30 make up just 7% of the civil service even though the age demographic makes up 23% of the total American workforce, according to Kupor. As of January 2026, young people made up 7.9% of federal employees, down from 8.9% in September 2024 before President Donald Trump took office, according to the Partnership for Public Service.

“I need young, smart people that are coming in, willing to serve,” Duffy said. “You can do it for a lifetime. You can make a career out of it, and that’s wonderful.

“I find it fascinating that more young people don’t want to apply,” he added . “We’re begging for people to come in.” 

The administration’s recruiting push has been undercut by an overhaul of the federal workforce when Trump first took office, according to Elizabeth Linos, the Emma Bloomberg Professor of Public Policy and Management at the Harvard Kennedy School. The slashes in headcount, as well as disruptions in workflow as a result of reduced staffing, are discouraging the next generation of talent from joining the federal workforce, she argued, even if DOGE has officially been disbanded for about a year.

“The…
items.t: ‘We’re begging’: DOGE slashed federal workforce to its lowest in 60 years, and the Trump administration says it still can’t recruit Gen Z workers

items.title: On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest
items.summary:
In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years . January’s benefits will be 3.6% higher, lifting the average retired worker’s monthly check to about $2,170, according to the Social Security Administration’s 2027 COLA announcement . The larger adjustment reflects persistent inflation in 2026.

Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first. Starting in January, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on Nov. 17 that the standard Part B premium rises by $6.50 to $209.40 a month. For most retirees, that premium is deducted straight from their Social Security benefit.

Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise. And because the premium is a flat amount, the smaller the check, the bigger the share it takes.

Smaller checks lose a bigger share of the raise 

For a retiree collecting the 2026 average of $2,095 a month, the 3.6% COLA adds about $75. After the higher premium, roughly $69 remains, so Medicare claims about 9% of the increase.

Lower down the scale, the bite grows. A $1,000 monthly benefit rises by $36, but only $29.50 survives the premium hike, an 18% haircut on the raise. At $1,500 a month, the COLA is worth $54 and the net gain is $47.50, meaning 12% of the raise goes to Medicare.

Bigger checks barely feel it. A $2,500 benefit gains $90 and keeps $83.50, losing 7% of the increase. At $3,000 a month, the raise is $108, the net gain is $101.50, and the premium takes just 6%.

That math applies to retirees who pay…
items.t: On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

items.title: Women’s soccer has a $1 billion opportunity—and the CEO of England’s top two leagues wants a slice of the pie
items.summary:
The 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup final was a watershed moment for women’s football, with record-breaking attendance and viewership numbers. More than 40 million people in North America tuned in to watch the U.S. beat China 5–4 on penalties in the final. Among them was ­ Canadian Nikki Doucet, then a student and college basketball player at St. Francis Xavier University. “That was the first time I’d seen women’s team sports on TV, and I remember feeling so excited,” she says.

Since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly. Its global fan base is projected to surpass 800 million by 2030, according to Nielsen Sports, while Fifpro expects the sport to be a $1 billion industry by 2027—a 72% increase from 2024.

Now CEO of Women’s Super League Football, the company responsible for operating the top two English women’s leagues (WSL and WSL2), Doucet is at the sharp end of that opportunity. England has become a commercial force in women’s football: Eight of the world’s 15 highest-revenue clubs are in the WSL, according to Deloitte, and Doucet believes the league is well-positioned to capture a “significant portion” of the potential $1 billion the sport is predicted to generate.

American entrepreneurs and investment groups are taking note. The success of the Women’s National Basketball Association—now an $850 million franchise—and the soaring valuations of teams in the National Women’s Soccer League (league leaders Gotham FC were recently valued at $350 million) underlines the potential. And many see an opportunity to buy in at an early stage in the commercial…
items.t: Women’s soccer has a $1 billion opportunity—and the CEO of England’s top two leagues wants a slice of the pie

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.t: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee

items.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
items.summary:
Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes?

In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north.

That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way.

items.t: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion

items.title: The 11 days that brought Jensen Huang back to Nvidia
items.summary:
Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out cofounder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak.

“There’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people,” Musk told the New York Times ’ Andrew Ross Sorkin, appearing at the newspaper’s DealBook summit via videoconference while Musk was in China with President Trump. “He has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades. He understands the technology incredibly well.”

Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return. 

“It is done,” he wrote. “The mistake has been corrected.”

Musk’s reaction reflects the extraordinary political muscle that he and other powerful figures in Silicon Valley and Washington flexed to bring Huang back. The Nvidia board reinstated Huang as CEO , the company announced Monday. His ouster, initially triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, has gripped the business and political worlds for the past two weeks, and his return promises more shock waves in the tech industry and the halls of power. Since Huang’s resignation was announced on Nov. 12, influential figures, from Musk to Trump , have waged a pressure campaign to make Huang CEO again, even as Nvidia’s board said it had moved on. Trump even called the board as it deliberated Huang’s reinstatement to push for his return. 

The reversal caps one of the most remarkable resurgences in business history, while raising numerous…
items.t: The 11 days that brought Jensen Huang back to Nvidia

items.title: ‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge
items.summary:
Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

What $156 billion looks like at $87.64 

TechCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the company’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares, and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

Because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch ’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

Three channels on three different clocks 

The largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund , a wholly owned LLC the company announced in…
items.t: ‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge

items.title: Why more Americans are choosing to pay over time
items.summary:
Paying with a credit card for lunch is routine today. It wasn’t always so. In a 1993 television report covering Burger King’s trial acceptance of credit cards, one customer objected, saying, “I think it’s pretty bad if you have to use a credit card when you go to a fast food restaurant. For something as little as $3.10.” Her objection assumed using credit for a small purchase meant you could not afford it. Newer payment tools face that same assumption today, even though the ways people manage everyday spending have changed. 

Today we see a major shift in how people across income levels access wages they have already earned and use deferred-payment options instead of traditional financing like credit cards. Block recently surveyed deferred-payment users, finding that 49% used cash advances or early wage access in the past year, alongside growing adoption of buy now, pay later. Survey findings also show about two in five Afterpay Pay in 4 and Pay Monthly users reported household incomes of $100,000 or more, underscoring that these tools reach across income brackets rather than serving only people without other options. 

The common thread behind both habits is timing. People often have money on the way that has not hit their account yet, and they use these tools to line up an expense with an incoming paycheck. By our estimate, U.S. workers at any given time have earned about $260 billion in wages they have not yet been paid. Among surveyed deferred-payment users, 65% financed an expense at least once in the past year because money was coming from a paycheck, refund, or…
items.t: Why more Americans are choosing to pay over time

items.title: ‘This seems like an extreme privacy violation.’ Surprising messages from the Muse AI agent are unnerving Meta’s own employees, report says
items.summary:
Meta employees have raised concerns about the company’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters . 

In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee posted.

A Meta colleague also shared that he got unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected and discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on Android phones, Reuters reported.

Another employee posted that during his chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, Muse said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

Other random Muse messages also took Meta workers aback, including a question about parental control over access to their child’s data and a conversation about picking up a coffee table that raised concern over “possible cross-account context leak.”

In response to the internal posts about Muse, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team said the agent appeared to be hallucinating, owing to built-in prompts that were designed to engage users between sessions, according to Reuters .

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that…
items.t: ‘This seems like an extreme privacy violation.’ Surprising messages from the Muse AI agent are unnerving Meta’s own employees, report says

items.title: Defense tech VC hit a record $37.9 billion last quarter. Two investors say it looks like 2021
items.summary:
When it comes to defense tech, it’s a FOMO-YOLO market, two prominent investors in the sector said onstage this week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

“I’m a long-term optimist, and I’ve been doing this for 30 years, but I see activity in the capital markets that reminds me of 2021,” said Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners.

“There are a lot of new entrants into the space. The death of SaaS and the disruption from AI has shifted capital into areas of deep tech, space, robotics, energy, and defense,” he said. “There’s folks deploying capital who aren’t experts in any one of those sectors. So, consequently, we can talk about a bubble.”

The money has arrived fast. Venture capitalists put a record $37.9 billion into defense tech across 269 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 117.5% from the prior quarter, according to PitchBook data cited by Fortune in its coverage of defense tech CEOs at the forum . Valuations have climbed with it: Early-stage defense startups have fetched 17 to 50 times revenue, Fortune reported this summer .

Even the sector’s biggest winners are uneasy. Anduril cofounder Trae Stephens told Fortune in June that mid-stage defense startups trade at multiples that are “completely disconnected from reality.” 

Aidan Madigan-Curtis, a partner at venture firm Eclipse, described the mood bluntly.

“There is a pretty big YOLO sentiment happening right now, essentially in physical tech investing,” Madigan-Curtis said. “There are a lot of tourist investors who are excited about a person, a background, a theme … [and] maybe…
items.t: Defense tech VC hit a record $37.9 billion last quarter. Two investors say it looks like 2021
